newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares near record in high volume.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares near record in high volume.

text.p: Russia's stockmarket opened the New Year with a bang, surging to near-record levels on Wednesday on all-time high turnover, and securities analysts predicted prices would advance throughout the month.

Equities turnover, a key indicator of market health in this relatively illiquid emerging market, reached $50.01 million on the Russian Trading System (RTS), besting the previous record of $46.97 million set on October 9, 1996.
The RTS 24-share index closed at 227.73, just shy of the record 227.79 set on July 4, 1996, the day after President Boris Yeltsin's re-election.

"People are going for liquidity but most of the money is going into stories that make sense," said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, pointing to leading shares such as utility Mosenergo and Surgutneftegaz oil company.
Both companies have made investment by foreigners and financial transparency company priorities.
Mosenergo, a bellwether of the Russian market, closed at a record high of $1.310, rising from $1.105 at close on Monday, the previous trading day.

Surgut, which on Monday announced details of plans for American Depositary Receipts, which allow foreign investors to buy shares while avoiding domestic settlement problems, accounted for over $15 million of trade in common shares alone.
Its ordinary shares closed at $0.600, up from $0.530 at Monday's close.
LUKoil, Russia's biggest oil producer, saw almost 300,000 shares change hands and closed at $13.10, up from $12.92.
Experienced and new investors in Russian equities were seen taking part in the bull market, which began over the Christmas and New Year holiday in thin trading.
The RTS index rose 16 percent between December 26 and Monday, January 6, partly on mark-ups by domestic brokers to close at 219.86.

Analysts said investors, including major new players such as U.S. pension funds, were investing chiefly among leading shares rather than secondary stocks which saw the strongest appreciation towards the end of 1996.
"People are going back to blue chips to get their core positions invested. After that people will start looking around again," Nail said.
Many dealers said the rally would continue through the month, breaking record highs.
But they said the rally would be corrected by a wave of selling when the pool of speculators and investors desperate to get into Russia evaporated.
"The question is, who will get nervous first -- those who have not put money in, or those who have the positions," said an analyst at a Western bank in Moscow.

"In the past, the Russians (with the positions) gave in first. I think we will see healthy demand, but not at these levels," he said, predicting leading stocks would ease four to five percent from early Wednesday prices.
Investors seem confident in Russia politically and economically, and increasingly willing to heed official statements, the analysts said.

The market, repeatedly rocked by rumours in the second half of 1996 that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had died, shrugged off presidential press service statements on Monday and Wednesday that Yeltsin had a cold.
"Unlike communist times, a president's cold does not mean he has been dead for three weeks," said Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Troika-Dialog bank in Moscow.
